definition.text: The basic unit of biological classification and a taxonomic rank, as well as a unit of biodiversity.

facts.text: A common definition is the largest group of organisms whose members can produce fertile offspring; others use karyotype, DNA sequence, morphology, behaviour or ecological niche.
A species is extinct when its last individual dies, but may be functionally extinct well before; over 99 percent of all species that ever lived are estimated to be extinct.
Species change by evolving into new species, exchanging genes with others, merging, or going extinct.
Difficulty assigning organisms reliably to a species threatens research validity, for example measures of how abundant a species is in an ecosystem.

title: Species concepts and the species problem

definition.text: The long-running dispute over how to define a species in a way that applies to all organisms.

facts.text: Most textbooks start from Ernst Mayr's 1942 biological species concept: interbreeding natural populations reproductively isolated from other such groups.

Other concepts include typological (fixed properties), phylogenetic (diagnosable lineages), evolutionary (own independent evolutionary fate), ecological (a set adapted to a niche) and genetic species.
The Mayr concept breaks down for asexual organisms such as bacteria, and for natural hybridisation and ring species, where gene flow links populations.
Microspecies complicate it too: perhaps 400 blackberry and over 200 dandelion microspecies in Britain alone.

contested_note: Biologists have not agreed on a single species concept.

definition.text: A population of organisms treated as distinct for purposes of conservation.

facts.text: The ESU, also called a wildlife species, shows how conservation can need units that differ from formal species concepts.
